metadata.title: Are You Supervising Claude at the Right Level?
metadata.topic: THREE LEVELS OF AI SUPERVISION · SHERIDAN-VERPLANK
metadata.purpose: Answer whether trusting AI 'the right amount' is a fixed personal habit or something that should scale with how much of a decision a given task actually hands over. Lands the carry-out that supervision is calibrated task by task, not a flat comfort level.
metadata.source_note: Source is a CLI-explainer build of a Sheridan-Verplank supervision classifier: Claude Code writes a script that classifies 8 AI interactions as Level I/II/III with a gap flag; demoed on Priya's 3 interactions (variable rename, market-size citation, architecture proposal) on a usage/supervision grid; revised to label the flag; re-run finds 4 of 8 flagged; closes with a run-it-on-your-own-history next step. Facts preserved: the 3-level framework (copy-paste/research/collaboration), Priya's grid and her 3 interactions, the calibrated-diagonal concept, the flag as short-checking-on-high-stakes, the run-your-own-history next step. Dropped: the Claude Code invocation, the Python script, the named classifier model (claude-3-5-haiku) -- general audience, no invented or stale product specifics. Register re-registered CLI/Teardown -> Plain; a wrong-guess beat, a one-flag beat (the 1978 framework applied to AI chat is an adaptation), and an anchor (Priya's own grid, literalized) were added per hai-simple's Phase 1 structure. See QUESTION.md for full detail.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B05 (Priya's 3 interactions on the usage/supervision grid)

beats.narration_text: Someone wonders if they're trusting AI the same amount every time. That's not quite it — the real question is whether you're trusting it the right amount, matched to the task. Liam explains.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Am I trusting AI the same amount every time?', hesitates on 'same', corrects to 'right', lands the real question

props.text:
Am I trusting AI
the same amount
every time?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('same' -> 'right') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: The natural assumption is that trusting AI the right amount means picking one comfort level and keeping it steady for every task. But renaming a variable and proposing a whole system architecture aren't the same task — one is quick and low-stakes, the other hands over a real decision. A fixed comfort level can't tell them apart, and the mismatch stays invisible until you actually compare what you asked for against how closely you checked it.

shot.new_visual_element: A single flat comfort-level gauge, struck; a variable rename beside a system-architecture proposal, wildly different weight

production_viz.label: One comfort level, or matched to the task?
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a card labelled 'ONE COMFORT LEVEL' holding a single unchanging gauge/dial that never moves. Right: a card labelled 'MATCHED TO THE TASK' with two small labelled blocks: 'rename a variable' (thin, light) and 'propose an architecture' (thick, heavy) — visibly unequal weight. The left card dims and gets a terracotta strike; the right card stays lit.

beats.narration_text: Sheridan and Verplank catalogued ten levels of automation back in 1978, for humans supervising machines generally. Applied to AI, three matter. Level One: copy-paste use — a quick edit you could just as easily have made yourself. Level Two: research-level use — you're leaning on it to gather or summarize something you'd otherwise have to dig for. Level Three: true collaboration — it's proposing the approach, not just executing yours.

shot.new_visual_element: Three stacked level cards, I / II / III, each lighting as named

production_viz.label: Three levels that matter
production_viz.mechanic: One card, three stacked rows connected by short arrows: 'LEVEL I -- copy-paste use', 'LEVEL II -- research-level use', 'LEVEL III -- true collaboration'. Each row lights in sequence as the narration names it; a small '1978' tag sits beside the card title 'SHERIDAN-VERPLANK'.

beats.narration_text: Take Priya, on one ordinary afternoon. She renames a variable — Level One — gives it a quick glance, fine, that's calibrated. She asks it to cite a market size — Level Two — and gives it the same quick glance. Below the line. She asks it to propose a whole system architecture — Level Three — and gives it that same quick glance again. Far below the line. Same glance, three very different amounts of trust handed over.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- usage/supervision grid, diagonal line, Priya's 3 dots: one on the line, two below

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- Priya's afternoon, one grid
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A square grid: x-axis 'USAGE LEVEL' (I to III), y-axis 'SUPERVISION GIVEN' (low to high), a diagonal line from bottom-left to top-right. Three dots appear one at a time, labelled as they land: 'rename a variable' lands on the diagonal and recolors teal ('calibrated'); 'cite a market size' lands below the diagonal and recolors terracotta; 'propose an architecture' lands far below the diagonal and recolors terracotta, inside a dashed box labelled 'FAR BELOW THE LINE'. THIS EXACT GRID COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B05.

beats.narration_text: The fix is a simple rule: flag any interaction where the checking was short but the task handed over the real decision — high stakes, barely glanced at. That's the dangerous case, not the careful one. One flag: Sheridan and Verplank never wrote this framework with AI chat in mind — applying their 1978 automation levels here is an adaptation, not something they specified themselves. It fits well enough to be useful, which is the only claim being made.

shot.new_visual_element: The flag rule as a single arrow; an explicit one-flag marker on the framework's fit

production_viz.label: THE ONE FLAG -- an adapted framework
production_viz.mechanic: A single rule card: 'SHORT CHECK' + 'HIGH STAKES' arrows converge into 'FLAG', drawn once and held. Beneath it, a smaller card labelled 'SHERIDAN-VERPLANK, 1978' with an arrow to 'APPLIED TO AI CHAT (this reel's adaptation)' -- a single terracotta FLAG marker over that arrow, the reel's only hedge, labelled as one.

beats.narration_text: Run the flag on Priya's afternoon and it catches exactly what you'd expect: the market-size answer and the architecture proposal both light up, the variable rename doesn't. But a flag doesn't prove the architecture proposal was actually wrong — it proves only that the checking didn't match what was handed over. And no flag on the variable rename doesn't prove nothing was missed there either — it just means this rule wasn't built to catch that kind of mistake.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- same grid, 2 of Priya's dots flag terracotta; splits into two both-directions cards

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- flagged, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B03 GRID RETURNS, identical placement. The two below-diagonal dots ('cite a market size', 'propose an architecture') each get a small terracotta FLAG tag; the on-diagonal dot ('rename a variable') stays teal, untagged. The grid shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'FLAG FIRES' with an arrow to 'CHECKING DIDN'T MATCH STAKES' -- NOT to 'ANSWER WAS WRONG' (struck through terracotta); right reads 'NO FLAG' with an arrow to 'THIS RULE DIDN'T CATCH IT' -- NOT to 'NOTHING WAS MISSED' (struck through terracotta).

beats.narration_text: Trusting AI the right amount isn't a fixed habit — it's calibrated to what you actually handed it, task by task.

props.quote: Trusting AI the right amount isn't a fixed habit — it's calibrated to what you actually handed it, task by task.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Look back at your last ten AI interactions and sort each into one of three levels: a quick edit, research help, or a real decision handed over. For any you call Level Three, say how many minutes you actually spent checking it. Anything under two minutes on a Level Three is the gap — ask what you'd need to check to close it. Liam, in for Bear.
